# Scope and prerequisites

This contest uses only techniques taught through section 41. See the lesson's
prerequisite table for their first teaching locations. The solutions combine
ordinary Fenwick trees, segment trees, lazy tags, offline sweeps, Euler
intervals, LCA, and insertion-only DSU. HLD, persistence, rollback, merge-sort
trees, and multidimensional Fenwick trees are not required.

A uses count-guided segment-tree descent from section 40. G uses an offline
value sweep. Every subtree update maps to one Euler interval; J has static
vertex values and uses root sums with LCA. Keep these contracts explicit when
assessing whether an earlier structure is sufficient.

# A. Dynamic Order Statistics

## Contract and reduction

Maintain frequencies on the score axis. Repeated scores occupy repeated ranks,
so a set cannot represent the answers. Section 40 already taught descending
a count segment tree to select the k-th active item; here a leaf can hold
more than one item. No Fenwick binary-lifting search is needed.

## Algorithm

```text
build an all-zero count tree over scores 1..m
insert x: increment leaf x and repair ancestor counts
erase x: decrement only if leaf x is positive
count <= x: sum the score interval [1,x]
k-th: reject if k exceeds the root count
       descend left if left.count >= k
       otherwise subtract left.count and descend right
```

## Sample walkthrough

The sample builds `{3,3,5}`. Rank two belongs to score `3`. Erasing one
copy leaves `{3,5}`, whose rank two is `5`. Counting scores at most `4`
before that removal gives `2`.

## Correctness

Each leaf is the multiplicity of its score; each internal node is the sum
of its children's counts. Insertions and valid removals preserve this by
repairing the leaf-to-root path. At a selection node, the first `left.count`
items belong to its left interval. Staying left or subtracting that count
therefore preserves the desired rank. At a leaf, its score is the answer.

## Complexity

Build `O(m)`; each operation `O(log m)`; memory `O(m)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Do not remove an absent copy, and do not deduplicate repeated scores.
Reject ranks above the total before descending. Test an empty multiset,
multiple copies at one score, scores `1` and `m`, and invalid ranks.

# B. Range Assign and Add

## Contract and reduction

The operation contract combines the lazy propagation of section 37 with two
update types. Addition and assignment do not commute. Keep a node sum, an
optional assignment, and an addition when no assignment is pending. A boolean
presence flag distinguishes assignment to zero from no assignment.

## Algorithm

```text
assign(node,x): sum = x*length; assignment = x; has_assignment = true; add = 0
add(node,x): sum += x*length
             if has_assignment: assignment += x
             else: add += x
partial operation: push pending tags to children, recurse, pull sums
full-cover query: return node.sum
```

## Sample walkthrough

The sample starts with sum `15`. Assigning positions `2..4` to `7` gives
`1,7,7,7,5`, sum `27`. Adding `-2` to positions `1..3` gives
`-1,5,5,7,5`, sum `21`; positions `2..3` sum to `10`.

## Correctness

The node sum describes its current interval, including its pending update.
An assignment replaces every prior value and pending update. An addition
shifts each value, so the sum increases by `x*length`; folding it into a
pending assignment describes the same transformation. Pushing applies that
transformation to both children, and pulling sums their disjoint intervals.
Induction on tree recursion proves every range update and sum query.

## Complexity

Build `O(n)`; every operation `O(log n)`; memory `O(n)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Applying assignment without clearing earlier additions changes update order.
Do not treat zero as an absent assignment. Test add-then-assign,
assign-then-add, overlapping intervals, singleton ranges, and negative values.
Use 64-bit sums, including the multiplication by segment length.

# C. Static Rectangle Count

## Contract and reduction

All sensors and queries are fixed, allowing the offline sweep of section 13.
For rectangle `[a,c] x [b,d]`, subtract the sensors in its y-range with
`x <= a-1` from those with `x <= c`. Compress y-coordinates and use a
Fenwick tree to count the active sensors in `[b,d]`.

## Algorithm

```text
create events (c,b,d,id,+1) and (a-1,b,d,id,-1)
sort sensors by x; sort events by their x bound
for each event X:
    insert every not-yet-inserted sensor with x <= X into the y Fenwick
    answer[id] += sign * (prefix(upper_bound(d)) - prefix(lower_bound(b)))
print answers by original query id
```

## Sample walkthrough

The first sample rectangle contains `(1,1)` and `(2,3)`, giving `2`.
The second contains `(4,2)` and `(5,5)`, also giving `2`. There is no
sensor on the third rectangle's row `y=4`, so its answer is `0`.

## Correctness

Before an event at `X`, the active set is exactly the sensors with `x <= X`.
This holds initially and is preserved by inserting all eligible sensors in
sorted order. The Fenwick prefix difference includes exactly y-values in
`[b,d]`. Subtracting the event at `a-1` removes exactly sensors left of the
rectangle. Each remaining sensor is counted once, including boundary points
and coincident sensors.

## Complexity

Sorting and processing cost `O((n+q) log(n+q))`; memory `O(n+q)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Insert sensors with equal x before answering an event at that x. Do not
require query boundaries to occur in the compressed coordinates. Use separate
lower and upper bounds for inclusive y-ranges. Test repeated points, a point
on each border, zero-width rectangles, and empty results.

# D. Nested Ranges Count

## Contract and reduction

Sort intervals by increasing left endpoint, breaking ties by decreasing right
endpoint. Use a Fenwick tree over compressed right endpoints. In a forward
sweep, earlier intervals with right endpoint at least the current endpoint
contain it. In a reverse sweep, later intervals with right endpoint at most
the current endpoint are contained by it. Identical intervals must be handled
as a group, because they count as containing each other.

## Algorithm

```text
sort (left ascending, right descending); group identical pairs
forward group of size s and right rank r:
    contained_by = seen - prefix(r-1) + s-1
    then insert all s copies
clear Fenwick
reverse group of size s and right rank r:
    contains = prefix(r) + s-1
    then insert all s copies
restore original interval order
```

## Sample walkthrough

For `[1,6]`, two copies of `[2,5]`, and `[3,4]`, the outer interval
contains three others. Each `[2,5]` contains its duplicate and `[3,4]`,
giving two; it is contained by the outer interval and its duplicate, also two.
The inner interval is contained by all three others.

## Correctness

In the forward sweep, every inserted interval has left endpoint no larger
than the current one. Its right endpoint is at least the current right
endpoint exactly when it contains the current interval. The reverse sweep
has the opposite left-endpoint condition, and its prefix selects exactly
contained intervals. Processing a whole identical group before insertion
avoids arbitrary within-group order; each member receives `s-1` contributions
from its other identical members and none from itself.

## Complexity

Sorting and both sweeps cost `O(n log n)`; memory `O(n)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Sorting equal-left intervals by increasing right endpoint breaks the sweep
condition. Inserting identical copies one at a time gives asymmetric answers.
Test all intervals identical, shared left or right endpoints, disjoint
intervals, and a deeply nested family.

# E. Subtree Add, Point Query

## Contract and reduction

Section 41 maps subtree `u` to one Euler interval. Adding to that interval
and querying a single position is the difference-array/Fenwick combination
from sections 4 and 36. Keep original values separately from accumulated
update differences.

## Algorithm

```text
record tin,tout with DFS
A u x: add +x at tin[u], and -x at tout[u] if within the array
Q u: original[u] + prefix(tin[u]) of the update difference array
```

## Sample walkthrough

Adding `10` to subtree `3` changes vertices `3,4,5`. Vertex `4` becomes
`14`, while vertex `2` stays `2`. Subtracting one from the root's subtree
then leaves vertex `3` at `12`.

## Correctness

Subtree contiguity makes each update an interval addition. Its two
boundary events contribute `x` to a prefix exactly at positions inside
that interval and zero outside it. Adding all preceding update events is
linear, so the prefix at `tin[u]` is the accumulated change to vertex `u`.
Adding its initial value therefore yields its current value.

## Complexity

Preprocessing `O(n)`; each operation `O(log n)`; memory `O(n)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

A preorder subtree interval differs from an entry-and-exit tour of length
`2n`. Handle the endpoint beyond the array explicitly. Test root updates,
leaf updates, negative additions, and overlapping ancestor subtrees.


Use iterative DFS for the input tree in C++ and Python so a long chain does
not exhaust the call stack. Segment-tree recursion has logarithmic depth.

```cpp
{{< include problems/e_subtree_add_point_query/solution.cpp >}}
```

# F. Dynamic Subtree Maximum

## Contract and reduction

The query is a subtree maximum, while updates assign a single vertex.
Flatten the rooted tree using section 41, then apply the ordinary point-update,
range-query segment tree of section 37 to the Euler array. No tree-path
decomposition is required.

## Algorithm

```text
flatten the tree; base[tin[u]] = initial[u]
build a maximum segment tree
U u x: assign base[tin[u]] = x
Q u: query maximum on [tin[u],tout[u])
```

## Sample walkthrough

Subtree `3` has values `3,4,5`, maximum `5`. Assigning vertex `4` to
`-10` leaves maximum `5`. Assigning vertex `5` to `-2` leaves values
`3,-10,-2`, maximum `3`.

## Correctness

The Euler interval contains exactly the subtree vertices. Each segment-tree
node stores the maximum of its interval. A point assignment changes one leaf;
recomputing ancestors preserves the invariant. Query nodes partition the
subtree interval, so taking their maximum gives the largest current subtree
value. A leaf query includes the vertex itself.

## Complexity

Build and flatten `O(n)`; updates and queries `O(log n)`; memory `O(n)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Zero is not a neutral maximum when values are negative. Assignment must
replace, not add. Test an all-negative tree, decreasing the unique maximum,
root and leaf queries, a single vertex, chains, and stars. DFS must be iterative
for the largest chains; segment recursion remains logarithmic.


Use iterative DFS for the input tree in C++ and Python so a long chain does
not exhaust the call stack. Segment-tree recursion has logarithmic depth.

## C++ reference solution

```cpp
{{< include problems/f_dynamic_subtree_maximum/solution.cpp >}}
```

# G. Subtree Value Count

## Contract and reduction

The values and all queries are static. Combine Euler intervals from section
41 with the offline threshold sweep from sections 13 and 36. Count values
at most `hi` and subtract
values at most `lo-1` inside the same subtree interval.

## Algorithm

```text
flatten the tree and sort vertices by value
query (u,lo,hi) creates (hi,u,id,+1) and (lo-1,u,id,-1)
sort events by threshold
before event T, activate all vertices with value <= T
activation adds 1 at that vertex's Euler position in one Fenwick tree
answer[id] += sign * count in [tin[u],tout[u])
```

## Sample walkthrough

Subtree `3` has values `4,2,3`; the interval `[2,3]` selects two.
The entire tree has two values in `[4,5]`. Vertex `2` alone has value `1`,
which is inside `[0,10]`.

## Correctness

At threshold `T`, the active positions are exactly the vertices with value
at most `T`. The Fenwick interval count restricts that set to exactly the
requested subtree. Subtracting the count at `lo-1` removes all values below
`lo`, while retaining values equal to either endpoint. Each vertex is
activated once and contributes separately even if values repeat.

## Complexity

DFS `O(n)`; sorting and sweep `O((n+q) log(n+q))`; memory `O(n+q)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Index the Fenwick by position, not value: values determine activation order,
positions determine membership in the subtree. Activate all equal values
before answering their threshold. Test duplicate values, `lo=hi`, no matches,
all matches, and negative bounds. Queries must be restored to input order.


Use iterative DFS for the input tree in C++ and Python so a long chain does
not exhaust the call stack. Segment-tree recursion has logarithmic depth.

# H. Incremental Connectivity

## Contract and reduction

Only edges are added, so this is precisely the DSU contract from section 18.
Maintain the connected components as disjoint sets. Use union by size and
path compression; neither reverse time nor rollback is necessary.

## Algorithm

```text
start each vertex in its own component
A u v: find both representatives; union them if different
Q u v: print YES exactly when representatives are equal
```

## Sample walkthrough

Initially `1` and `3` are separate. After edges `1-2` and `2-3`, they
share a component. Vertex `4` remains separate until edge `3-4` is added.

## Correctness

Initially the components are isolated vertices, matching the empty graph.
Adding an edge connects the two endpoint components and no others, exactly
the effect of a DSU union. If they are already equal, a repeated edge or
self-loop changes no component. Induction over insertions proves that the
DSU sets are exactly the graph's connected components at every query.

## Complexity

Initialization `O(n)`; all operations `O(q alpha(n))` amortized;
memory `O(n)`. Here `alpha` is the inverse Ackermann function.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Do not count a repeated edge as a new component merge. A vertex is connected
to itself even without edges. Test repeated edges, self-loops, a growing
chain, isolated vertices, and queries before the first insertion.

```cpp
{{< include problems/h_incremental_connectivity/solution.cpp >}}
```

# I. Subtree Assign, Add, and Sum

## Contract and reduction

Compose the Euler mapping from section 41 with the lazy sum tree used in B.
The new task adds a tree-shaped query set; its assignment/addition semantics
are unchanged. Convert each subtree to one interval, then reuse B's invariant.

## Algorithm

```text
flatten the tree and build the Euler array
1 u x: lazy-assign interval [tin[u],tout[u]) to x
2 u x: lazy-add x to that interval
3 u: query its sum
compose and push assignment/addition tags as in B
```

## Sample walkthrough

Subtree `3` initially sums to `12`. Assigning `7` to it gives
`7,7,7`; adding `-2` to the leaf subtree of `4` leaves `7,5,7`, sum `19`.
Vertices `1,2` add `3`, so the entire tree sums to `22`.

## Correctness

Euler contiguity gives exactly the affected vertex set for each operation.
B's tag rules assign or add the specified amount to every entry in that
interval, maintaining every node sum. Since the Euler mapping is one-to-one,
the interval sum equals the sum of the subtree's current vertex values.
The mapping and the lazy-tree proof establish separate parts of correctness.

## Complexity

Flatten and build `O(n)`; each operation `O(log n)`; memory `O(n)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Keep interval conventions consistent: these implementations adapt B's
inclusive 1-based segment-tree interval to `[tin[u]+1,tout[u]]`.
Test assignments to zero, an ancestor assignment after a descendant addition,
the opposite order, leaves, and whole-tree operations. Use 64-bit products.


Use iterative DFS for the input tree in C++ and Python so a long chain does
not exhaust the call stack. Segment-tree recursion has logarithmic depth.

# J. Static Vertex Path Sums

## Contract and reduction

The vertex values never change, so root-prefix sums suffice alongside LCA
from section 41. Let `S[u]` include every vertex from root `1` through `u`.
For `w=lca(u,v)`, the required sum is
`S[u]+S[v]-2*S[w]+a[w]`.

## Algorithm

```text
DFS: compute parent, depth, and S[child] = S[parent] + a[child]
build the usual binary-lifting ancestor table
for query u,v:
    w = lca(u,v)
    print S[u] + S[v] - 2*S[w] + a[w]
```

## Sample walkthrough

For query `2,4`, the LCA is `1`: root sums are `3` and `8`, so
`3+8-2*1+1=10`. For `4,5`, the LCA is `3`; the answer is `4+3+5=12`.
For `3,3`, the formula returns `a[3]=3`.

## Correctness

The two root prefixes both contain the root-to-`w` prefix. Subtracting it
twice leaves the two branches strictly below `w`; neither branch contains
`w`. Adding `a[w]` restores that shared endpoint once. The two branches and
`w` partition the simple path, proving the formula, including `u=v`.

## Complexity

Preprocessing `O(n log n)`; each query `O(log n)`; memory `O(n log n)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Do not apply an edge-distance formula directly to inclusive vertex values:
the shared ancestor must be restored. This formula relies on static values;
assignments would invalidate precomputed root sums. Test equal endpoints,
ancestor endpoints, negative sums, an LCA at the root, and a long chain.


Use iterative DFS for the input tree in C++ and Python so a long chain does
not exhaust the call stack. Segment-tree recursion has logarithmic depth.

## C++ reference solution

```cpp
{{< include problems/j_static_vertex_path_sums/solution.cpp >}}
```

## Python reference solution


# K. Static Weighted Rectangles

## Contract and reduction

Reuse C's offline rectangle reduction, but insert the weight of each point
rather than the count `1`. The point set is fixed; this task needs only one
ordinary Fenwick tree. Negative weights do not affect the sweep order.

## Algorithm

```text
sort fixed points by x; compress their y coordinates
create +1 event at c and -1 event at a-1 for each rectangle [a,c] x [b,d]
insert each eligible point's weight at its y rank
for each event, accumulate its sign times the Fenwick sum in [b,d]
restore query order
```

## Sample walkthrough

Weights `5` and `-2` at `(1,1)` contribute `3` together. Including the
point of weight `4` at `(2,3)` gives the first answer `7`. The second
rectangle includes only that point, giving `4`; the third gives `3`.

## Correctness

The active Fenwick prefix is the sum of weights with bounded x and y,
because each eligible point is inserted exactly once. Prefix subtraction
selects the inclusive y-range. Subtracting the event at `a-1` removes the
contribution from points left of the rectangle. This is a linear identity
for weights of either sign, and coincident points remain separate contributions.

## Complexity

Sorting and processing `O((n+q) log(n+q))`; memory `O(n+q)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Use 64-bit Fenwick sums and answers. Do not discard negative weights or
combine coincident points by keeping just one weight. Query bounds can be
absent from compression. Test cancellations, all-negative weights, coincident
points, degenerate rectangles, and coordinates near both extremes.

# L. Subtree Add, Subtree Maximum

## Contract and reduction

Map subtrees to Euler intervals and use section 37's lazy range-add tree
with a maximum summary. Uniform addition preserves which value is largest:
`max(a_i+x)=max(a_i)+x`. Thus adding to a fully covered node changes its
maximum by `x`, rather than by `x*length` as a sum tree would.

## Algorithm

```text
flatten the tree; build maximum summaries
apply(node,x): maximum += x; pending_add += x
partial operation: push pending_add to both children; clear it; recurse
A u x: range-add on [tin[u],tout[u])
Q u: range-maximum on that interval
```

## Sample walkthrough

Subtree `3` starts with maximum `5`. Adding `5` gives values `8,9,10`,
so the whole-tree maximum is `10`. Subtracting `20` from the whole tree
leaves subtree `3` at `-12,-11,-10`, maximum `-10`.

## Correctness

Each node maximum includes all updates covering its full interval. Applying
a uniform addition shifts that maximum by exactly the added amount.
Pushing shifts both child summaries, preserving their actual values; merging
with maximum restores the parent summary after partial updates. Euler
contiguity selects exactly the subtree vertices, so the range operation has
the required effect and returns exactly the subtree maximum.

## Complexity

Flatten and build `O(n)`; each operation `O(log n)`; memory `O(n)`.

## Implementation notes and targeted tests

Adding `x*length` to a maximum confuses it with a sum. Push before a
partial query as well as before a partial update. Zero is not a neutral
maximum. Test all-negative answers, root additions followed by leaf queries,
nested subtree updates, cancellation, chains, and stars.


Use iterative DFS for the input tree in C++ and Python so a long chain does
not exhaust the call stack. Segment-tree recursion has logarithmic depth.

```cpp
{{< include problems/l_subtree_add_maximum/solution.cpp >}}
```

# Stress testing and what to carry forward

The package generators compare against direct multiset/array scans, explicit
subtree enumeration, path reconstruction, rectangle scans, and graph searches.
These oracles avoid reproducing the optimized decomposition. Fixed samples
check the stated examples; random tests emphasize boundaries and update order.
Use large chains and large operation counts to check stack safety and cost.

Run both reference languages with:

```bash
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/42_advanced_data_structures_mixed/check.py --keep-going
```

Carry forward the habit of proving the mapping separately from the stored
invariant. The same established structure answers different questions after
a valid reduction, but a convenient-looking interval or prefix formula is
not sufficient without that proof.
